stories.body:
Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege

A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.

Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China . With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.

Wang remained jailed without bail on Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.

US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.

The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.

“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”

Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.

The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.

Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.

Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.

The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.

He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.

Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.

Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.

It is not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only.

Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

stories.title: Trump commercial railing against his enemies kept airing after court blocked it
stories.summary: US attorney apologized to court, said government has stopped running Trump ads.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US attorney apologized to court, said government has stopped running Trump ads.

Trump commercials paid for by the US government continued airing on TV the day after a judge blocked the ads because they likely violate a US law against government-funded publicity or propaganda.

In the most widely aired commercial, Trump railed against his perceived enemies and said he would “liberate America from these villains once and for all.” The campaign also included a commercial praising Trump’s record as president, another in which Trump calls the US the “most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history,” and commercials related to the Iran war and the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

US District Judge Jennifer Rochon issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) blocking the ads on Sunday, October 11, which took effect at 6:45 pm that night. The order said the government must cancel the ads, “including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026.”

The Trump administration had told the court on October 10 that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) advertising purchases were set to expire on October 11 and would not be renewed. Despite that, the ads continued airing the night of October 11 and on part of October 12. This was also a week after Trump’s October 5 statement that he would start paying for the ads “myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”

A US attorney yesterday filed a status report saying that the government is now complying with the order and issued an apology. “As Your Honor is aware, the Court emailed the TRO to the parties yesterday at 6:46 p.m.,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald wrote in a filing . “Counsel for the Government emailed the TRO to agency counsel at 7:58 p.m. Agency counsel did not become aware of Government counsel’s email until this morning. The undersigned apologizes to the Court and the plaintiffs.”

The ads aired as part of a $20 million purchase order that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) made on September 20 with LMD Agency, an ad firm. The DHS told the court that the ad placements through October 11 cost $19 million.

Trump admin said ads would stop Sunday

In the previous Trump administration filing opposing the motion for a temporary restraining order, one of the government’s arguments was that a court order was unnecessary because the ads would not run past October 11. It said:

DHS issued a purchase order to obtain media services from a vendor in support of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for placing national media buys. The vendor has currently purchased media buys under the terms of the purchase order through tomorrow, October 11, 2026. DHS has directed the vendor not to make any additional media buys past October 11, and DHS has no plans to make any additional media buys under the purchase order or otherwise use appropriated funds on any similar contracts for the creation or distribution of the media that is the subject of this lawsuit. Accordingly, the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow, and Plaintiffs therefore will suffer no harm, let alone irreparable harm, absent an injunction.

The Washington Post reported yesterday that the ads kept running after the restraining order took effect. Nonprofit advocacy group Common Cause and other groups that sued the government submitted a filing later in the day notifying the court of the government’s noncompliance.

The Trump ads continued airing on programs including 60 Minutes , ABC World News Tonight , and America’s Funniest Home Videos . They ran nearly 400 times after the restraining order took effect, including 32 times on Monday, according to AdImpact data cited in the plaintiffs’ court filing.

“Plaintiffs do not presently seek contempt sanctions,” the groups said. “But given that the ads have continued to run on October 12—the day after Defendants insisted the ad-buy was no longer effective—Plaintiffs request a status conference to determine Defendants’ compliance.”

Judge: Ads “are purely partisan”

After the government filed its status report, Rochon scheduled a hearing for Wednesday “to discuss this and next steps in this action.” The lawsuit is in US District Court for the Southern District of New York.

The plaintiffs are Common Cause; Robert Hunter, a Democratic candidate for a state legislature seat in Alabama; Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ; and Empire State 32BJ SEIU PAC. Defendants include DHS, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and the Executive Office of the President.

Rochon found that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in their claim that the Trump administration violated the 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act requirement that no funding may be used “for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress.”

“Defendants do not contest that the at-issue advertisements are purely partisan and unconnected to DHS’s official functions,” Rochon wrote. “Thus, the Court finds that Moving Plaintiffs are likely to succeed in showing that the advertisements are impermissible ‘publicity or propaganda’ under Section 718 [of the Consolidated Appropriations Act].”

Trump recycled ad from 2024 campaign

One of the ads “is almost identical to one used during President Trump’s 2024 campaign, other than the fact that its funding disclaimer now identifies the United States government rather than his presidential campaign,” Rochon wrote. “It depicts President Trump walking down a hallway while delivering a series of statements about his political adversaries. Among other things, he promises to ‘demolish the deep state,’ ‘drive out the globalists,’ ‘cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,’ ‘throw off the sick political class that hates our country,’ and ‘rout the fake news media.’ This advertisement provides no information about DHS’s official functions.”

As of October 8, the ad “had aired approximately 9,679 times, generating an estimated 972 million impressions at an estimated cost exceeding $9.09 million,” Rochon wrote. Another $6.3 million was estimated to have been spent on four other government-funded ads challenged in the lawsuit. That’s about $15.4 million as of October 8, and more was spent over the next few days.

Rochon found “a clear and substantial likelihood” that the Trump administration violated the Administrative Procedure Act “because Congress did not appropriate funds for DHS to spend on disseminating the challenged advertisements.” Rochon said a restraining order was necessary despite the DHS claim that it had “no plans” to continue running the ads.

“Defendants also have not provided reasonable assurances that OMB will not reapportion funds from another source to continue running similar advertisements,” she wrote.

The temporary restraining order is in place for only two weeks, but it can be converted into a preliminary injunction that would keep the ads off the air while litigation continues. Trump, the White House, OMB, and DHS face a similar lawsuit filed by the Democratic National Committee in the federal court in the District of Columbia. A hearing on a motion for a temporary restraining order in that case is scheduled for Thursday.

stories.title: BA flight forced to turn back over cracked window
stories.summary: British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick and passengers were due to resume their journey.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
File photo of a British Airways plane

Published 13 October 2026

A British Airways flight en route to Portugal was forced to return to Gatwick Airport on Tuesday due to a minor technical issue, reported to be a cracked window.

Flight BA2660 was heading to Faro in the Algarve but diverted over north-western France in order to return to London Gatwick.

AirNav Radar, a flight data provider, posted on X that "a passenger window is cracked. Flight deck going through checks before deciding were to divert".

A spokesperson for British Airways said the plane landed safely at Gatwick due to a "minor technical issue" and passengers were due to resume their journey.

"We have apologised to customers for the delay to their journey, and our teams are working hard to get their travel plans back on track," they said.

Airnav Radar reported that the BA Airbus A321 squawked the 7700 emergency code, which is used when there are mechanical or technical problems on board aircraft.

Last week, a BA flight bound for Chicago spent five hours circling over Ireland, before turning back and landing at London Heathrow, where it had taken off.

The flight issued an emergency alert and passengers reported oxygen masks dropped in the cabin, as well as turbulence. Tracking data showed it rapidly descended from 37,000 feet to 9,000 feet.

And in August Serbian national Ljubisa Karović's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the window on a Ryanair flight, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock".

Ryanair subsequently said the window may have been damaged by a foreign object.

US inflation jumps to 3.7%

Newsflash: US inflation jumped in September, and by more than expected, as the soaring cost of motor fuel pushed up the cost of living.

The US Consumer Prices Index roses by 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% in August. Economists had forecast a smaller rise, to 3.6%.

Prices rose by 0.6% in Spetember alone.

Gasoline prices jumped by 9.1% in September, and were 34% higher tha a year ago, as motorists across America felt the impact of Donald Trump’s Middle East war at the pumps.

Those price pressures prompted Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin last Friday – but as reported earlier , it’s not expected to unlock much extra supplies to the market.

Wall Street is falling

Stocks are falling at the start of trading on Wall Street, as today’s US inflation report disappoints investors.

The S&P 500 sharesindex has fallen by 0.4%, shedding 32 points to 7,773 points.

The tech-focused Nasdaq is down 0.5%.

US bond yields jump

US government borrowing costs are pushing higher, after today’s inflation report hardened expectations of interest rate rises from the Fed.

The yield on two-year Treasury bills has risen by 13 basis point (0.13 of a percentage point) to 4.92%, hitting their highest level since 29 September.

Ten-year US Treasury yields are up 9.5bps to 5.3% – towards the 24-year highs set earalier this month.

This adds to the fiscal mess facing the US ( something the IMF warned about this morning ); high bond yields push up the cost of servicing the $40tn US national debt, and makes issuing new debt more expensive too.

Congressman Brendan F. Boyle is blaming Donald Trump’s trade war, and his war with Iran, for driving up costs for Americans.

Boyle , a Democratic member of the House of Representatives, posted on X:

double quotation mark President Trump promised to lower costs on “day one,” but American families have already paid $3,500 more due to inflation since he took office. If he cared at all about working people, he would end his tariff taxes and his reckless Iran war.

Dollar hits 18-month high

The US dollar has hit an 18-month high, as traders anticipate that today’s inflation reading could prompt an increase in US interest rates.

The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of currencies, is up 0.5% to its highest level since April 2025.

October interest rate hike 'back in play'

This jump in inflation increases the chances that the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates later this month.

According to CMEFedwatch , a quarter-point Fed rate hike in October is now a 43% chance, up from 22% yesterday.

Stephen Brown , Chief North America economist at Capital Economics , says:

double quotation mark The upside surprise to core CPI in September was broad-based rather than due to any obvious temporary factors, therefore bringing an October rate hike back into play and presenting upside risks to our forecast for just two more 25 bp hikes from the Fed.

Quilter: 'Ugly US inflation data' is blow to Trump

Today’s higher than expected inflation reading is “a blow to Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterms”, says Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot.

It could also encourage the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, which would not please Trump at all.

In a note headlined “Ugly US inflation data may shift Fed into more aggressive hiking mode”, Carter explains:

double quotation mark The President has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy. “CPI came in at 3.7%, slightly above expectations, and similarly core inflation was above predictions, suggesting that prices are feeding into the wider economy. Fuel and energy do remain the primary driver of inflation and certainly explains the actions of the US administration of late. “This data is going to heap a whole lot of pressure on the Federal Reserve. Any chance of cuts to help with a stumbling labour market have essentially been vanquished with such elevated levels of inflation. The conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved any time soon, and as such, the current levels of inflation will likely remain well into 2027. “Bond yields have been under scrutiny in recent weeks as those inflation concerns harden, and this will do little to appease the market. It is not inconceivable that ten-year treasury yields continue to march higher. Indeed, today’s data means another rate hike this year from the Fed cannot be ruled out as it may need to get more aggressive in its policy decisions in order to quell other inflationary trends.”

US core inflation up too

In a worrying sign, core inflation across the US has also risen.

The inflation measure which strips out food and energy costs rose to 2.6% in the year to September, up from 2.4% in August.

That could be a sign that inflationary pressures are broadening, which would concern central bankers.

George Brown, senior economist at Schroders, says:

double quotation mark “While energy prices might be grabbing the headlines, today’s report suggests the inflation problem runs much deeper. A stronger-than-expected core inflation reading adds to mounting evidence that domestic price pressures are becoming more entrenched, rather than easing. “Markets are right to assume that policy will need to become much more restrictive to return inflation to target. The question is whether the Fed is prepared to tighten as much as the inflation outlook demands.”

The cost of energy across the US jumped by 5.2% during September, today’s inflation report shows, and was 20% higher than a year ago.

The shelter index (which tracks the cost of housing) rose 0.4% in September after rising 0.3% in August.

The index for food was unchanged in September, with the cost of food at home down 0.1% but the cost of food away from home up 0.2%.

On an annual basis, food prices were 2.5% higher than a year ago.

Those price pressures prompted Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin last Friday – but as reported earlier , it’s not expected to unlock much extra supplies to the market.

The US-Russia diesel deal might not lead to much more diesel on the market, but it’s a boon to Moscow’s economy.

Russia’s deputy prime minister Alexander Novak told reporters that the deal will boost Russia’s economy and allow it to increase production and refining volumes.

He added:

double quotation mark “Without a doubt, this is a positive signal for our economy.”

[Reminder: the IEA warned this morning that the lack of operational Russian refinery capacity means Trump’s deal won’t make a big difference to the diesel market].

Euro hits 16-month low against the pound

Back in the financial markets, the euro has dropped to a new 16-month low against the pound.

Sterling rose over €1.1850 this morning, the highest since June 2025.

The US-Russia diesel deal can pave the way for further economic cooperation between the two countries, Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said today.

Dmitriev added that Moscow would overcome any sanctions-related difficulties to ensure the diesel supplies.

The example of diesel cooperation with the US “will open other opportunities as well,” he told reporters, Reuters reports .

Back in Thailand, foreign secretary Ed Miliband has promised a ‘pragmatic approach’ to energy extraction in the North Sea.

Speaking to Sky News after speaking on the sidelines of the IMF’s annnual meeting, Miliband said:

double quotation mark “I’ve always had a pragmatic approach to the North Sea. We continue to use oil and gas for decades to come. The North Sea continues to play a role. We’ve also got to make progress when it comes to climate and show leadership working with others.”

I’m not sure ‘pragmatic’ is the very first word that the fossil fuel industry would use to describe Miliband, who as energy secretary ruled out new North Sea oil and gas exploration or lower taxes for fossil fuel companies .

But! Yesterday he reportedly approved a massive new oil field development in waters around the Falkland Islands, much to Argentina’s chagrin.

We’re still waiting for the government’s decision on whether to approve the controversial Rosebank and Jackdaw fields in the North Sea…

Burnham condemns Green Party's 'antisemitic' Zionism declaration

Published 4 minutes ago

Andy Burnham has said he will not support his party forming a partnership with the Green Party as long as it maintains a policy of defining Zionism as a form of racism.

Speaking in the House of Commons, the prime minister said the motion, backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month, was "wrong" and "antisemitic" and Labour would have "nothing to do with it".

The motion said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive".

Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" and that he had wanted to see it amended.

However, he has defended the substantial part of the motion arguing that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

The motion, having been backed by members, has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

The subject was raised during Prime Minister's Questions, when Conservative MP Dame Harriett Baldwin urged Burnham to "rule out co-operating" with the Green Party.

Burnham replied: "Can I condemn the motion that was passed unequivocally.

"It is wrong, it is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it.

"We will always take the right response when it comes to any partnerships we have with other parties.

"We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds the position that has recently been adopted."

Labour is currently in coalition with the Green Party on some local councils including Sheffield.

A Downing Street spokesman would not confirm if the prime minister's position extended to local areas or just applied to national government level.

The adoption of the motion has prompted some Green Party figures to call for changes to the party's rules.

Last week, MP Ellie Chowns told the BBC: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the 230,000 members in the party.

Key backer of the motion Lubna Speitan has defended the motion arguing that it aimed to oppose "racist systems of oppression" adding: "We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions."

stories.title: The Paris Auto Show is full of interesting cars Americans can’t have
stories.summary: Small EVs and efficient people carriers update familiar names for the modern age.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Small EVs and efficient people carriers update familiar names for the modern age.

Perhaps the days when auto shows debuted new models aren’t entirely over. The big trade shows for cars were a gateway drug for many, expos where you could see the newest models of today and the concepts of tomorrow. But automakers increasingly got tired of sharing the spotlight with each other. New reveals moved offsite to events the night or even the week before the show itself. One by one, brands pulled out of auto show after auto show until there was little left to see . And then the pandemic hit.

But the news out of Paris, where its auto show held media day yesterday, seems like we stepped back into a time when automakers would debut new cars aplenty. That retro vibe extends to the cars themselves, with plenty of familiar nameplates reimagined.

France’s Renault has a long and glorious history of delightful concept cars, and more on what it brought to Paris later. But the star of the show was arguably Stellantis, with strong work from Citroen, Peugeot, and Fiat, to name but three. But this article is meant to irritate you, because I’m pretty sure none of the stuff you’re seeing here will come to the United States. And it’s doubly irritating considering what Stellantis’ brands do offer us over here, doubling down on the same malign trends I saw back in 2020 : did you know they’re about to relaunch a V8 Hellcat-powered Charger ?

EVs can be small and cheap, apparently

The European concepts show us that, as those Kneecap chaps have it, there’s a better way to live. A sense of utopia was responsible for the original Citroen 2 CV; it had to be cheap enough for a farmer to buy it and rugged enough to get produce to market without breaking it. I’m not sure whether the 2 CV Concept also has to be able to transport eggs across a rutted field without breaking any (although the glove box is a clue), but Citroen says that affordability, lightness, practicality, and versatility were top of mind during the design process. The press release probably didn’t need to also say the company imbued it with distinctive character or charm; that’s quite obvious from the design.

The interior feels particularly refreshing compared to the touchscreen overload we’re usually presented. It might be stripped back, but it still has plenty of whimsy—the display in front of the driver has a bande dessinée theme, and the radio is portable and removable from the car. Technology fans don’t despair, there’s still the 8-inch touchscreen, but this too features more of Belgian comic artist Jean-Luc Delvaux’s work.

I’m even confident some of that whimsy will make it into production, because Citroen is going to build the 2 CV within the next two years, it says, and at a starting price of just 15,000 euros ($16,766). That slots it between low-speed microcars like the Renault Twizy, Citroen Ami, and the Fiat Topolino (which you can buy if you live in Michigan), and superminis like Volkswagen’s Polo.

And as it happens, VW had a new electric ID. Polo to show off in Paris, along with an affordable electric ID. Cross crossover. Together with the closely related Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, VW Group says it has more than 150,000 orders already for its new “Electric Urban Car Family.”

Audi’s first attempt at a supermini was the esoteric A2, an aluminum and aerodynamic experiment from the wild days of Ferdinand Piëch. Like the original, the Audi A2 e-tron is an efficient little thing—its most efficient car ever it says, with a WLTP rating of 4.9 miles/kWh (100 km/12.8 kWh). As one might expect, I was a big fan of the original A2, which was always a rarer sight on the roads than it deserved to be. I can definitely see that car in the A2 e-tron’s design, and the promised efficiency sounds impressive even if there might not be quite the same excessive and cost-ineffective overengineering under the skin. I can’t see any way that Audi brings this car to America, just like we never saw the first A2, or the A1.

The Peugeot 205 GTi was a Gallic alternative to the late ’80s-era Golf GTIs that Americans will be familiar with, and it’s into this well that Peugeot dipped for Paris. Or rather, the wild 205 T16 Group B rally homologation special that the 205 GTi gave birth to, a car that won the world Rally Championships in 1985–86. Like the Renault 5 Turbo 3e from last year, the E-T16 Concept shows us that hatchbacks needn’t just be humble devices for running errands; they can excite, too. I’m not entirely sure about that multifunction steering wheel, though.

What if I need something bigger?

“But Jonathan, I don’t live a block from a metro station, and I need something a bit bigger to cope with my family,” you say. It is true that cars like the 2 CV or ID. Polo will be too small for some. This is true for Europeans as well, and both Renault and Fiat had something for these segments.

The original Fiat Multipla is another underappreciated car from the late ’90s. The styling was challenging for some, but it was a masterclass in space efficiency, seating six in two rows of three abreast. Rather than simply copying that, but with a slab of batteries under the cabin, the Fiat Multiplay explores the idea of a vehicle that’s adaptable, transforming from a three-row people carrier to a pickup. The front passenger seat can be reconfigured as a lounger, and there’s a “Petsenger” seat—a modular mounting point that allows you to swap in a pet bed, child’s car seat, storage compartment, or small table.

The original Renault Espace was very much loved and created the people-carrier segment out of thin air, at least in Europe. The familiar one-box shape remains for the new E-Space Concept, though with massive 23-inch wheels at the corners, the proportions are a little more Hot Wheels or Matchbox than the 1984 version. (Even in Europe, car designers are drawn to oversized wheels.)

There is a criminal lack of electric minivans on the market today, and the only one available here in the US is the VW ID. Buzz. And that sold so poorly that VW suspended imports for a model year. Which probably tells you how likely a US launch for a production E-Space would be.

Final inflation report before voters go to polls comes amid widespread anger over cost of living under Trump

Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections

Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday.

US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.

Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%.

Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually.

Price increases this year have largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to soar. Average gas prices remain over a dollar per gallon more than last year, according to data from AAA. Meanwhile diesel, which powers domestic supply chains, reached a record-high last month.

September’s inflation rate is the highest it has been before a midterm election, with the exception of the pandemic, since 1990.

The economy has consistently been cited as a top issue for American voters, as rising gasoline prices and persistent inflation have eaten into household budgets. Higher energy prices from the Iran war have cost Americans over $1,020 per household, according to Brown University , and a total of $133bn for all US consumers.

Much of the anger is expected to be directed at Republicans, who control Congress and the White House. According to a recent survey from Reuters/Ipsos, 78% of Americans blame the current Trump administration’s policies for inflation that is outpacing their earnings, including 57% of Republicans who support Donald Trump.

In recent weeks, Trump has attempted to downplay his administration’s role in price increases, pointing to the Iranian government as the cause of the squeeze. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest inflation report.

On Tuesday, Trump posted on social media that Yemen’s Houthi group was attacking Saudi Arabia in a deliberate effort to affect the upcoming elections.

“They’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran…in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE,” he wrote.

Heightened inflation will put more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates, its tool to cool prices. Last month, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, citing elevated prices. Higher rates affect the cost of borrowing money, including mortgage rates. The 30-year mortgage rate, applied to the most commonly used loans for home ownership, is up to 7.40%.

“Inflation in the US has come in higher than expected, in a blow to Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterms,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, in a statement. “The President has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy.”

stories.body:
Exclusive: Business secretary says he will not change trade rules due to EU pressure and denies UK will become a ‘back door’ for cheap imports

The business secretary has hit back at European demands for British tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the government will not change its trade rules because of pressure from Brussels.

Jonathan Reynolds warned that the government would not bow to calls from other countries for the UK to hit Chinese vehicles with import taxes, despite political pressure to align with the EU in exchange for deeper future economic ties.

The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 and last Friday agreed a 350,000 a year quota on Chinese hybrid cars amid fears cheaper alternatives are causing deindustrialisation and job losses.

Reynolds conceded that levying sanctions on Chinese goods was an option in the future, but he dismissed concerns from Brussels that the UK could provide a back door to the European market.

His comments highlight the divisions that remain between the UK and EU on trade and industrial policy, which could derail the prime minister’s attempts to move closer to Brussels.

“I just want to be clear: when we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that,” said Reynolds during a trade trip to India.

“In 2024, [we] looked at this issue carefully, and we keep it under review depending on what the needs of industry are … But it comes down to what is the fundamental nature of the UK automotive sector. It’s an export-led sector, so that’s what I’ve got to take into account.”

With Europe having imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese electric cars, some believe that the UK has opened an alternative route into the EU for Chinese companies setting up in the UK to sell into the bloc.

Nissan, for instance, has agreed to look at building cars in northern England for the Chinese manufacturer Chery .

Reynolds rebutted those accusations, however, saying: “The UK currently has no major Chinese manufacturer based in its automotive sector, so we’re not making vehicles here and sending them to the single market through some sort of back door.”

His comments raise the stakes ahead of intense final weeks of negotiations before the long-awaited UK-EU summit, which Andy Burnham confirmed this week would be held in Brussels on 20 November.

The prime minister told the Commons on Monday he wanted a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s place in Europe, as he framed the summit as a possible first step to EU membership.

The new Made in Europe trade rules aim to protect European companies from subsidised Chinese imports, but British manufacturers worry they will also be shut out of supply chains.

The issue will not formally be on the agenda at the November summit, but British officials are hoping to use those talks to shape the European legislation.

Diplomats on both sides of the Channel say the summit will now be an early test of whether Burnham’s desire for a “real reset” in UK-EU relations is likely to bear fruit.

One EU official said this week that the UK’s negotiating position would determine whether it was worth pursuing more fundamental changes such as British access to the single market, a new customs union or re-accession.

Some in Brussels have been pushing for Britain to levy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in return for getting access to the European market under the new trade rules.

Reynolds has previously dismissed such an option in part because of the risk that Beijing could hit the UK with reciprocal tariffs, damaging British companies such as Jaguar Land Rover.

He said it would be to Europe’s detriment if it did not admit the UK into the scheme. “If you look at the impact analysis of such a policy, the consequences for the EU [of] excluding the UK are much more difficult,” he said.

“This is not just in the UK’s interest; it’s not in the EU’s interest because obviously we have integrated supply chains.”

Reynolds said the summit was an important milestone in EU-UK relations but also insisted that new trading terms for electricity, emissions and food and drink products would be a major achievement in themselves.

Speaking from a two-day trade delegation to Delhi and Mumbai, he acknowledged that the landmark free trade agreement he helped strike last year with India would become defunct if Britain does rejoin the EU.

“Obviously, if you enter those arrangements, you are doing things collectively. So there would be trade relationships with the UK that were based on Europe, the EU as a whole – that is how the European Union works in terms of its relationship.

“That’s why obviously when we were part of it, we didn’t have these separate bespoke arrangements.”

But he insisted that it remained worth continuing to push to broaden the scope of the agreement, as he unveiled a series of UK-India investments which officials say are worth over £1bn to the UK over the next 15 years.

The deal has already begun to reduce the price of Scotch whisky in Indian shops, after tariffs were reduced from 150% to 75%. Now British officials are keen to free up trade in services as well as goods, for example, pushing for both countries to recognise each other’s legal qualifications.

“There are some specific things regarding who can practice law and in which area,” Reynolds said. “I am confident over the medium to long term that this will improve over time.”

He added: “We’ve got to be cognisant of this long-term position with the EU. But frankly, there’s a job to be done here and now, which we’re doing.”

stories.title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
stories.summary: The prime minister has been under growing pressure since the club was found guilty of Premier League rule breaches.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) chats to Andy Burnham in 2019 at the Etihad Stadium, when he was mayor of Greater Manchester

Published 14 October 2026, 11:06 BST

Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.

The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.

Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.

The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.

On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.

The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.

It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".

But the statement did not specify that this referred to , external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.

A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality.

Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699.

Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.

But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.

Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts Published 29 September

BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.

Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.

But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount.

Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City.

"This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football."

And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners".

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester".

"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."

Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me."

With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club".

When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.

The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned.

In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations.

The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.

Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict.

Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).

Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.

EFF and the ACLU of Northern California represent SIREN and CAIR California, two non-profits that serve San Jose residents, in this case. stories.summary: When we communicate online today – from your personal emails and DMs to secure international commerce – we usually do so with encryption. Encryption converts readable data into unreadable gibberish to protect our privacy and security. This didn’t just happen organically. Three decades ago, the U.S government treated encryption like a weapon, and it took some unlikely heroes to set it free: a grad student, a junior lawyer, and a fledgling digital rights group who sued the federal government. The ruling in Bernstein v. Department of Justice held that code is speech and so is protected by the First Amendment – a precedent that underpins the internet as we know it today. stories.title: US inflation rises more than expected ahead of midterm elections
stories.summary: The pace of price rises increased to 3.7% in the year to September, driving by higher motor fuel costs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 October 2026, 13:47 BST

US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.

The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.

Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have spiked following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.

The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US.

What is inflation?

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

What causes inflation?

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

What is the current rate of inflation?

Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices.

Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.

In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics.

Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.

Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.

At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.

How have tariffs affected inflation?

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

US President Donald Trump raised tariffs

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

What tariffs has Trump introduced and why? Published 22 August

Has inflation been worse lately?

While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.

During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.

Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.

Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.

Can inflation ever go down?

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect prices to fall further. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

stories.title: Operation Vivaldi: success of Ukraine’s counteroffensive shows it has learned to manoeuvre on a drone-filled battlefield
stories.summary: Russia’s drone and missile attacks on Ukraine’s population and infrastructure continue to dominate coverage of the conflict. But on the ground, Ukraine has been making significant, if still limited, gains. In mid-September, Ukraine formally announced the existence of Operation Vivaldi , which has retaken territory near Lyman and disrupted a Russian advance toward the fortified cities that form a key part of Ukraine’s eastern defences. What’s important isn’t just that Ukraine has been conducting a successful counteroffensive. It is how it has created the conditions for success and what that might say about future battlefield dynamics in the Russo-Ukraine war . Lyman is a road and rail junction on the northern approaches to Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Russia has spent months trying to advance around it as part of a wider effort to encircle Ukraine’s eastern defensive line. Vivaldi has substantially reduced the Russian push into Ukrainian territory north of Lyman, disrupting the northern arm of the plan. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has claimed that by the end of last month the operation had retaken 176 sq km of territory. How Operation Vivaldi played out on the frontline in Ukraine. Institute for the Study of War Vivaldi is significant because it has been much more than a brief attack against Russian forces. The scale of the preparations, the use of lessons from previous operations and the coordination of several brigades make this an exercise in planning and carrying out a large-scale military campaign . stories.body:
Russia’s drone and missile attacks on Ukraine’s population and infrastructure continue to dominate coverage of the conflict. But on the ground, Ukraine has been making significant, if still limited, gains.

In mid-September, Ukraine formally announced the existence of Operation Vivaldi , which has retaken territory near Lyman and disrupted a Russian advance toward the fortified cities that form a key part of Ukraine’s eastern defences.

What’s important isn’t just that Ukraine has been conducting a successful counteroffensive. It is how it has created the conditions for success and what that might say about future battlefield dynamics in the Russo-Ukraine war .

Lyman is a road and rail junction on the northern approaches to Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Russia has spent months trying to advance around it as part of a wider effort to encircle Ukraine’s eastern defensive line. Vivaldi has substantially reduced the Russian push into Ukrainian territory north of Lyman, disrupting the northern arm of the plan. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has claimed that by the end of last month the operation had retaken 176 sq km of territory.

Vivaldi is significant because it has been much more than a brief attack against Russian forces. The scale of the preparations, the use of lessons from previous operations and the coordination of several brigades make this an exercise in planning and carrying out a large-scale military campaign .

Vivaldi began in May this year, but Ukraine kept it quiet until September. The corps described its first phase – which appears to have taken place over several months – as creating favourable conditions for later activity. This involved attacking Russian air defence, electronic warfare capabilities, artillery and logistics, disrupting Russian drone operations and concealing Ukrainian intentions.

Ultimately, Ukrainian forces were able to disrupt Russian defences well beyond the frontline and into the depth of the Russian rear areas, and drive back Russian drone units, including elements of the elite Rubicon drone formation . This allowed Ukraine’s Third Corps to achieve the necessary measure of local drone superiority.

Subsequent phases exploited this advantage with the coordinated application of different military capabilities. Drones and robots have been important. Drone crews and other units worked together to strike enemy systems before the infantry advanced. And ground robots carried supplies, conducted mine clearance or provided fire support, and some, for the first time, were dropped by drones behind Russian defences.

But other capabilities have been critical. Even armour, in the form of tanks and infantry fighting vehicles, has retained a role – although it is used more cautiously because of the threat posed by enemy drones. After other forces have suppressed enemy drone and artillery units, armoured vehicles have helped exploit gaps in the enemy defences, allowing troops to advance much faster.

Coordinated offensive

But the important development is the manner in which these elements have been coordinated. What has made Vivaldi stand out is much more about how established and newer capabilities have been brought together through innovative tactics and techniques than it is about the impact of a single system.

These lessons may be already being put into practice beyond Lyman. Ukraine has also been making gains east of the fortress-belt cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk . This has included advances across the Siverskyi Donets river – which was an important target for Russia back in January 2026. These counterattacks are also likely to have been supported by extensive preparation.

This suggests that Ukrainian forces are applying some of the same methods elsewhere. What this means for the war, though, is still a matter of debate. One of the central difficulties faced by both sides in the conflict is how to escape from a static war of attrition and restore manoeuvre to the battlefield. Operation Vivaldi provides evidence of the methods that might work to restore the power of offensive operations on a high-visibility, high-precision battlefield.

Important caveats

But there are some caveats that must be considered. First, 176 sq km is still a limited advance in the overall scheme of the war. And Russia is continuing to advance elsewhere, albeit very slowly.

Second, while Russian milbloggers – the ecosystem of journalists, commentators and analysts who support the war, but can be critical of the way it is being waged – have confirmed the problems caused by Operation Vivaldi, we are still reliant for most of our information on Ukrainian sources. The formation conducting the assault, Third Corps, is adept at information operations , which promotes its successes relative to the performance of other units.

Third, to have a broader impact, the successful techniques will have to be transferred across other Ukrainian units . This has not always proved easy.

Fourth, Russia is likely to adapt, given that the capacity to adapt to new equipment and tactics is one of the significant features of the war . Russia’s military planners are likely to study the operation and try to copy or counter what has worked. It may strengthen its defences, seek to blunt Ukrainian drone and electronic-warfare advantages, and apply some of the techniques to its own offensive operations.

How far and how fast it can adapt will therefore be a defining factor in the impact of Operation Vivaldi. At the moment, Russia is moving troops from other sections of the front. Its response, however, has been heavily criticised in the Russian milblogger community, especially because of the culture of “beautiful reports”: the propensity across the Russian military to avoid reporting failure upwards and to exaggerate the effectiveness of Russian operations.

Meanwhile, Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure have intensified ahead of winter. And Kyiv has claimed that Putin will seek to increase its mobilisation to raise another 300,000 troops for the battlefield.

It seems unlikely, given its limited scale, that Vivaldi has prompted these developments. But the operation is still unfolding. Whether Ukraine can repeat the methods, and whether Russia can adapt to stop it, will determine whether this operation remains a local success or whether it points to a larger change in the direction of the war.

stories.title: These Women Were Trying to Escape Domestic Abuse. ICE Detained Them Instead.
